newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS - Pacific BBA starts US export harvest.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Pacific BBA starts US export harvest.

text.p: Australian automotive parts and plastics group, Pacific BBA Ltd, cut the first blooms of its U.S. export strategy on Tuesday when it posted a 27 percent rise in first half net earnings to A$12.6 million.
The company, whose brakes unit PBR exports park brakes and aluminium calipers to North America, said its sales revenue grew by 15 percent to A$262 million in the six months to June 30.
"PBR is now beginning to reap the benefits of the years of product and market development and the capital expenditure programme," Pacific BBA chief Barry Jackson said in a statement.

Jackson said the group was confident of seeing increased sales and earnings in its second half driven by higher automotive export volumes and improvement in the Australian and international brake servicing markets.
"We believe we are on track to achieve our profitability goals. There is nothing out of line with what we thought it would be," he told a media briefing.

The company had strong growth plans in place for PBR and its construction and industrial products division, Webforge, and was in the process of determining how to expand its newly acquired wire products group, Melwire, into Asia, he said.
Pacific BBA earlier announced that PBR won a deal to supply disc brake calipers to a vehicle manufacturer in Thailand and would build a plant there to fill the order.
The company said it would invest A$13 million in land, buildings and plant in Thailand and expected production to start in mid-1998 with full production reached by the year 2000.
"Although it is not a big investment, strategically this is a very important step for us as it is another piece in our global manufacturing base," Jackson told the briefing.
It said capital spending was expected to lift gearing above 70 percent by year-end from 51 percent at June 30.
The rise in debt was mainly attributable to to the funding of the construction of the group's A$100 million brake caliper plant in Knoxville, Tennessee, with debt reducing in 1998.
The company said the construction of the Knoxville plant was on schedule and should be completed by the end of 1997 with production due to commence in mid-1998.

Pacific BBA has said it expected its U.S. order books to be boosted by A$60 to A$70 million in 1998 when the plant starts production. The company hopes to find a partner to take a 49 percent stake in the operation.
One black spot on the group's first half earnings was the performance of its plastic division which suffered from lower volumes in Australia and strong competition from imports.
The division's sales fell five percent in the half while earnings before interest and tax dropped 42 percent.
The company said its industrial textiles business, Sarlon, was a poor performer in the division and it was reviewing its investment in this business.

"Sarlon always loses money in the first half. It's seasonal. It makes all its money in the second half - we need to get volume through that facility or we will sell it to someone who can," Jackson said at the briefing.
Jackson said Pacific BBA was running out of patience with Sarlon but was not blaming the management, rather the tough market for its products and competition from imports.
"We'll fix it in the next six months one way or the other," he said.
Pacific BBA shares closed six cents higher at A$5.70.
-- Melbourne Bureau 61-3 9286-1435
